posts.title: Paid vs Free-to-Play: How Monetization Shapes Game Design

children.t: Many premium games today promise dozens — sometimes hundreds — of hours of gameplay.But after a few hours, players often realize that much of that time is spent repeating familiar tasks: clearing camps, collecting scattered items, or completing structurally similar side missions.
If paid games don’t rely on retention the same way free-to-play games do, why do they still lean so heavily on repetitive design?
The answer is not simply about creativity or lack
lies deeper — in how different monetization models fundamentally shape design priorities.
Designing for Value vs Designing for Retention
At a high level, premium and free-to-play games optimize for very different goals:
aim to justify a one-time purchase
This difference creates two distinct design philosophies:
And this is where repetitive structures in premium games begin to make sense.
For premium games, especially AAA titles, there is an implicit expectation:
A $60–$70 game should last dozens of hours.
This creates what can be called
Developers are not just designing gameplay —they are designing
As a result, design often shifts toward:
“Can this mechanic scale to fill 40 hours?”
Not because designers lack ideas,but because
repeatable structures are the most reliable way to produce large volumes of content.
AAA game development is, at its core, a form of industrial production.
Be produced efficiently by large teams
Low system variety, high content volume
High variety, high density of unique experiences
From a production standpoint, this is logical.From a player perspective, it can feel like sameness.
Failure cannot easily be recovered through live updates or monetization loops
A safe 8/10 experience is often better than a risky 6/10.
Repetition, in this sense, becomes a form of stability.
Interestingly, free-to-play games often feel more “varied” moment-to-moment — even though they are highly system-driven.
That’s because their goal is not to deliver a long continuous experience, but to:
However, this comes with its own trade-offs:
Systems are often built around monetization triggers
Progression pacing may be artificially stretched
Design serves retention more than expression
So while F2P games may feel more dynamic in the short term,they are often
more constrained at a systemic level
Repetition Is Not a Failure — It’s a Trade-off
It’s easy to criticize repetitive mission design in premium games as lazy or uninspired.
But in reality, it is often the result of deliberate trade-offs:
Repetition is not a design failure — it is a structural consequence of the business model.
This leads to a more interesting question:
Many of the most memorable games are not the longest ones —but the ones where every moment feels intentional.
Perhaps the future of game design lies somewhere in between:
Monetization does not just affect how games make money —it shapes how they are designed, structured, and experienced.
Understanding this helps us move beyond surface-level criticismand toward more thoughtful discussions about the future of game design.
Because in the end, the question is not just:
“What kind of system is this game designed to serve?”

posts.title: How can AI help us with game designing?

children.t: AI Won't Design Your Game — But It Will Change How You Do It
Over the past year, while working on Unity projects and building gameplay systems, I started to notice a growing gap between
. Game design is not just about creativity—it is about iteration, system balancing, and constant testing.
At the same time, AI tools have rapidly evolved. From generating code to creating art assets, it seems like AI can “do everything.” This naturally raises a question:
Can AI actually help us design games?
The short answer is: yes—but not in the way most people expect.
AI is not replacing game designers. Instead, it is fundamentally reshaping how game design is done—especially in prototyping, content creation, and tool development.
1. Rapid Prototyping: Reducing the Cost of Ideas
Game design is inherently iterative. Most ideas don’t work the first time—they need to be tested, adjusted, and sometimes discarded entirely.
Help implement quick UI or interaction prototypes
In my own workflow, especially when experimenting with small gameplay mechanics, AI significantly reduces the time needed to go from
. Instead of spending hours writing boilerplate code, I can focus on testing whether the idea itself is fun.
AI reduces the cost of iteration, which is the core of game design.
This is not about replacing developers—it’s about accelerating exploration.
2. Content Generation: From Inspiration to Raw Material
AI is also powerful in generating creative content:
However, one important reality is often overlooked:
Raw AI-generated content is not production-ready.
In real game pipelines, assets must go through structured processes—whether it’s proper material setup (e.g., PBR workflows), animation integration, or performance optimization.
AI outputs are best treated as:
For example, an AI-generated environment concept might guide level design, but it still requires human decisions to ensure gameplay clarity, navigation, and performance.
AI helps you start faster—but finishing still requires design thinking.
3. Tooling and Pipelines: The Real Impact of AI
From my experience, the most meaningful impact of AI in game design is not in generating content—but in
In my previous work, I built:
A path editor for level design
These tools significantly improved iteration speed for designers and developers.
Now imagine integrating AI into this workflow:
However, there is a critical engineering principle:
AI should not directly control the game engine. It should operate through a structured middleware layer.
Instead of letting AI manipulate low-level systems, we can:
This aligns with modern AI integration practices, where systems use abstraction layers to ensure stability and prevent unpredictable behavior.
In other words, AI becomes a
, not a replacement for the engine.
Game design is not just about isolated features—it is about systems:
AI can generate individual ideas, but it often struggles to understand how systems interact over time.
A combat mechanic may seem interesting in isolation
But it might break pacing, difficulty, or resource balance
These are system-level decisions that require holistic thinking—something AI currently lacks.
2. No Real Understanding of Player Experience
Through my own project experience, especially in narrative-driven games, I realized that
AI can assist in building systems—but it cannot evaluate emotional impact.
In complex systems like Unity or Unreal, this becomes a real engineering risk.
To make AI usable in production, we must constrain it with:
Modern approaches emphasize making AI outputs
, rather than treating them as black-box solutions.
Without these constraints, AI becomes more dangerous than helpful.
The Future: AI as a Co-Designer
Looking forward, AI will not replace designers—but it will redefine the design process.
The future workflow may look like this:
We are already seeing early forms of this in advanced pipelines:
This is not about replacing creativity—it’s about scaling it.
AI is often presented as a revolutionary force that will “design games for us.” In reality, its role is much more practical—and much more interesting.
AI will not replace game designers—but designers who use AI will replace those who don’t.
The future of game design is not human vs AI.
, working together to create better, faster, and more meaningful experiences.

posts.title: Is Gaming a Superior Narrative Medium? Rethinking Storytelling Across Forms

children.t: For a long time, I believed that games were the ultimate narrative medium.

Compared to books and films, games seem to have everything: text, visuals, sound, and most importantly, interaction. They appear to be a natural evolution—a medium that absorbs all previous forms and adds agency on top of them. From this perspective, it felt almost obvious that games should be
However, after spending a semester developing a narrative game called
At first glance, games seem powerful because they combine multiple channels of information. But in practice, having more expressive tools does not guarantee a stronger narrative.
In fact, many games fail precisely because these elements are not in harmony.

Text, visuals, sound, and gameplay often exist in parallel rather than in integration. The player may read dialogue, watch cutscenes, and perform mechanics—but these layers do not reinforce each other. Instead of deepening the experience, they fragment attention.
In those moments, games can actually be

A novel, with only text, can guide the reader into an intensely focused mental space. There are no competing systems—no mechanics pulling you away, no UI demanding attention. The reader is free to fully engage with the author’s intention.
This kind of concentration is surprisingly difficult to achieve in games.
To explain what I learned, I need to first explain the game we were trying to build.

is a 3D narrative experience about a middle school teacher trapped in a time loop, reliving the day of a devastating earthquake. The player returns to the school again and again, trying to understand what happened—and whether anything can be changed.
The game is structured around two interconnected spaces:
, where the earthquake unfolds in real time (a short, intense window of around 96 seconds)
, representing fragmented memories and emotional aftermath
Each loop, the player gathers more information:Who died? Why did they die? What choices led to those outcomes?

At first, the player acts blindly. But over time, knowledge accumulates, and the player begins to make deliberate decisions—choosing who to save, where to go, and what to do within a very limited timeframe.
There are multiple ways to “solve” each situation:
A more optimized solution (requires exploration and planning)
A narrative-driven solution (requires understanding the character and context)
Eventually, the player can save everyone.
But in the final moment, the game reveals a truth:
These people were never actually saved.
The entire experience is about confronting memory, guilt, and acceptance. The player is not changing the past—but learning to understand it.
While building this system, I realized something fundamental:
A game becomes powerful only when
playing it is equivalent to understanding it
, the time loop is not just a mechanic—it
Optimization reflects the human desire to “fix” the past
Discovery reflects the process of reconstructing memory
The player does not just watch a story about regret—they
regret, again and again, until meaning emerges.
This is something books and films cannot fully replicate.
However, reaching this level of integration is extremely difficult.
Even in our own project, we constantly struggled with questions like:
Are players focusing on solving puzzles, or understanding characters?
Does the time pressure enhance emotion, or reduce reflection?
Are mechanics reinforcing the theme, or distracting from it?
It is very easy for gameplay and narrative to drift apart.
And when they do, the experience weakens.

This is why many games, despite having rich audiovisual elements, fail to deliver a coherent narrative experience. In contrast, books and films—precisely because they are more constrained—can achieve a stronger sense of focus.
There are games that successfully achieve this integration.
Titles like The Last of Us, BioShock Infinite, and Red Dead Redemption 2 demonstrate how mechanics, world design, and narrative can reinforce each other.
Every playthrough becomes a continuous reinforcement of the story.
It requires not only technical skill, but alignment across design, art, narrative, and production. It also requires scale—something that is often impossible for small teams.
Because of this, books and films are not replaced by games.
They remain powerful precisely because of their limitations.
A book can guide thought with precision.A film can control rhythm and emotion through editing and framing.
Games, on the other hand, give up control in exchange for agency.
Without careful design, it can dilute meaning rather than strengthen it.
So, are games a superior narrative medium?
I no longer think the answer is simply yes.
Most games are not stronger than books or films.
game has the potential to surpass them.
Games are not inherently more powerful—they are
When mechanics, narrative, and player experience align, games can create something unique:
Not just observing a story, but
changed how I think about storytelling.
The question is no longer whether games are better.
If we can, then games are not just a combination of media.
They are a fundamentally new form of expression.

posts.title: Successful Narrative Games---When Gameplay Becomes Story

children.t: Many games claim to be “story-driven,” but in reality, their stories live outside of gameplay.

The emotional moments happen in cutscenes. The character development happens in dialogue. The themes are delivered through scripted events. Gameplay, meanwhile, functions as a challenge system — something the player completes in order to unlock the next piece of narrative.

In the most powerful story games, gameplay is not separate from narrative. The mechanics themselves express character, theme, and conflict. The player does not simply witness the story — they enact it. The rules of the system become the language of storytelling.

When gameplay becomes story, removing the cutscenes would not remove the emotional experience. The meaning of the narrative would still be present in the way the player moves, fights, manages resources, makes decisions, and inhabits the world.
This blog explores how certain games achieve this integration — not by attaching narrative to gameplay, but by designing mechanics that
I. The Common Mistake — Story as Decoration

Many so-called “narrative games” still treat story as something layered on top of gameplay. The emotional beats happen in cutscenes. The character arcs unfold in dialogue sequences. The theme is explained through scripted scenes. Meanwhile, gameplay exists in a separate space — as combat, traversal, puzzles, or progression systems that operate independently from the narrative.
In these cases, story and gameplay coexist, but they do not interact.

If you removed the cutscenes from such a game, the gameplay would still function. You could still shoot, jump, level up, or solve puzzles. But the emotional meaning would largely disappear. The systems themselves would not carry the weight of the story.
This separation creates a structural gap.
Gameplay becomes the “work” the player performs in order to unlock narrative rewards. Story becomes a decorative layer that justifies mechanics, rather than something expressed through them.

As designers, this is a tempting structure. It is safer. We can write a strong script and build a functional system without forcing them to speak the same language. But this separation also limits the medium. It reduces games to interactive movies with mechanical intermissions.
The most powerful narrative games break this pattern.
They do not ask: “How do we attach story to mechanics?”They ask: “How do we design mechanics that
That distinction is small in wording — but enormous in design implication.
If gameplay can become story, then mechanics must do more than create challenge — they must generate emotional experience.
, survival is not simply a narrative theme. It is a mechanical condition. The systems are designed to make survival feel heavy, uncomfortable, and morally complicated.
is not just difficulty tuning. It is emotional architecture.
Healing costs resources that could have been used elsewhere.
Stealth is often safer than combat — but slower and more tense.

The game forces players into uncomfortable trade-offs. Every decision carries weight: Do I spend this bottle to distract an enemy, or save it for crafting? Do I risk confrontation, or avoid it entirely?
The scarcity system does something powerful: it makes violence feel expensive.
This is not a heroic power fantasy. It is attrition.
The mechanics embody the world’s cruelty. The narrative does not have to repeatedly tell you that survival is brutal —
the system makes you feel it
Joel does not fight like an action hero.
His animations are slower. Melee combat is messy. Enemies do not fall cleanly. Gun recoil feels heavy. Struggles are prolonged.
Joel is not designed as a symbol of mastery. He is a tired survivor.
If combat were fluid and stylish, it would contradict the story. Instead, the friction in the mechanics reinforces who Joel is.
You do not just learn about Joel through dialogue — you inhabit him through constraint.
The Hospital Sequence — When Action Becomes Moral Statement
The final hospital sequence is often discussed in terms of narrative choice. But what makes it powerful is not the cutscene — it is the action.
The player must carry Ellie out.

The game does not present this as a dialogue option. It presents it as gameplay. You cannot remain neutral. You cannot skip it. You must perform the act.That design choice transforms the player from observer to participant.The moral ambiguity is not something you watch. It is something you enact.And because you enacted it, the emotional weight belongs to you.This is the moment when gameplay fully becomes story.
, narrative does not sit above mechanics. It is embedded within them. Scarcity creates emotional tension. Combat weight expresses character. Forced action creates moral implication.
The systems are not supporting the story. They are telling it.
III. Structural Mechanics as Narrative Theme
is not survival. It is inevitability. Fate. The illusion of choice.
And instead of merely telling that story through dialogue, the game builds it into its structure.
Early in the game, players are presented with small choices:
Pick a brooch or a bird.
At first, these choices appear meaningful. But as the narrative unfolds, the game reveals a disturbing pattern: no matter what you choose, certain outcomes remain constant.
“There’s always a man. There’s always a lighthouse. There’s always a city.”
The game is not offering branching narrative freedom. It is demonstrating constrained variation.
This is not a flaw. It is thematic design.
The structure of limited choice mirrors the theme of determinism. The gameplay system quietly reinforces the narrative argument: you are moving forward, but you are not truly free.
In many games, death is a mechanical reset. In
When Booker dies, the player does not simply reload. Instead, Elizabeth pulls him into another version of reality.
The respawn mechanic is narratively justified.
This is structural alignment: the rules of the system are the rules of the universe.
Death does not contradict the story — it confirms it.
The multiverse theme is not only explained through exposition. It is experienced through repetition, alternate realities, and structural loops.
Unlike many RPGs that promise freedom,
There are no radically branching storylines. No diverging endings based on player morality.
The lack of branching becomes part of the argument.
The game asks: What if your perception of agency is only structural containment?
Instead of designing for maximum freedom, the game designs for thematic consistency.
Here, the constraint itself becomes narrative.
, gameplay does not generate emotional survival tension. Instead, it builds a structural metaphor.
Limited choices express determinism.Respawn expresses multiverse logic.Linearity expresses philosophical constraint.
The system architecture becomes thematic architecture.
When structure aligns with story, gameplay becomes narrative argument.
IV. Three Design Conditions for Gameplay Becoming Story
, we can identify three conditions under which gameplay truly becomes narrative.
If the theme is survival, the mechanics must create vulnerability and scarcity.If the theme is determinism, the structure must limit freedom.
Mechanics are not neutral systems. They carry emotional and philosophical meaning.
A mechanic becomes narrative when the player’s action expresses something beyond efficiency.
, pulling the trigger in the hospital is not just a combat action — it is a moral
, continuing forward despite the illusion of choice reinforces inevitability.
When players feel responsible for what happens, gameplay transforms into storytelling.
allows players to feel the theme through interaction.
You do not need a character to say “this world is cruel” when scarcity makes you hesitate to use your last
do not need a monologue about fate when the structure of the game denies meaningful divergence.
When the system teaches through experience, gameplay becomes narrative lan
Successful narrative games do not attach story to mechanics as decoration. They align mechanics with theme, structure with philosophy, and player action with emotional consequence.
In these games, cutscenes enhance the experience — but they are not the source of meaning. The meaning lives inside the rules.
When gameplay becomes story, narrative is no longer something we watch unfold. It is something we perform.
For designers, this shift changes everything. Story is not written after systems are built. Story is built into systems from the beginning.
And when that alignment happens, the medium reaches its full expressive potential.

feels almost perfect to me. At its core, the game is deeply strategic, but instead of separating strategy and randomness, it tightly connects them. Randomness is not added on top of strategy; it is embedded inside every strategic decision. This design gives me strong satisfaction when I dynamically adjust my strategy in response to change. The constant thinking this requires fully engages my brain and makes the game deeply addictive.

, randomness is rarely uncontrolled. Many minion effects use randomness, but always within clear limits. For example, a minion might deal damage to a random enemy minion, summon a random minion with a specific cost, or transform a minion into another minion of the same cost. Even though the exact outcome is uncertain, the possible results are clearly defined.
Because of this, when I play these minions, I usually know what
happen, even if I do not know what
happen. I am not guessing blindly. I am making a strategic choice based on a known range of outcomes. This turns randomness into a decision about risk, not luck.
2.Numbers That Favor Long-Term Thinking (Board State over Single Result)

are designed so that their value comes from long-term advantage, not from one perfect outcome. A minion that deals random damage might not hit the ideal target every time, but over many games, using it at the right moment often leads to positive results.

For example, playing a random-damage minion when the opponent has multiple low-health minions increases the chance of a good outcome. This rewards players who understand board states rather than those who hope for perfect luck. Strategy becomes about timing and probability, which keeps my thinking active throughout the match.
3. Randomness After Player Choice (Playing the Minion Is the Decision)
the player commits to an action. I choose when to play a minion, whether to trade first, and how much mana to invest. Only after I make these decisions does the random effect trigger.

For example, if I play a minion that attacks a random enemy, I could first remove a dangerous target or reduce the number of possible enemies. The random result may still be unpredictable, but the situation leading to it is created by my choices. This makes the outcome feel earned, even when it is not ideal.
4.Forcing Constant Strategic Adjustment (Minions Change the Board, Not End the Game)

Most random minion effects do not immediately decide the game. Instead, they change the board state by altering health values, removing or creating minions, or shifting tempo. Each of these changes creates a new situation that demands a new plan.

When a random effect produces an unexpected result, I have to quickly reassess whether I should play aggressively, defend, or save resources. This constant need to adapt is exciting. The strategy does not stop after one decision; it continues as the board evolves.
5. A System That Rewards Learning (Knowing the Minion Pool)

works because it exists within a learnable system. When a minion summons or transforms into another minion, it draws from a known card pool shaped by the current expansion and meta. Over time, I learn what kinds of minions are likely to appear and which outcomes are dangerous or safe.

This knowledge directly improves my decisions. I am not just reacting emotionally to randomness, but actively predicting outcomes based on experience. This learning process strongly engages my brain and makes each match feel meaningful.
6.Emotional Engagement Through Numbers (Minion Swings and Comebacks)

Random minion effects often create dramatic board swings. A lucky or unlucky result can change the flow of the game, but because these effects are tied to player decisions, the emotions feel justified. When a random effect works in my favor, it feels rewarding. When it fails, I can usually see how I might have played differently.
This balance between surprise and responsibility keeps me emotionally invested without feeling cheated. It encourages reflection rather than frustration, which makes me want to keep playing.

demonstrates that randomness does not weaken strategy. Through careful numerical tuning and minion effect design, randomness becomes a core part of strategic play. By embedding uncertainty into every decision, the game constantly challenges players to adapt. This mental challenge fully engages my brain and is the reason the game feels so satisfying and addictive to me.

posts.title: Why a 22-Minute Loop Can Feel Bigger Than an Open World

children.t: I’ve played plenty of games that try to impress me with size: bigger maps, more quests, more loot, more upgrades.
did something completely different. It gave me a tiny slice of time, told me it would end no matter what I did, and somehow made me feel more free than most “open world” games ever have.
That’s the design question I can’t stop thinking about:
Why does a fixed-length time loop feel so attractive? Why is repeating the same time window not boring—sometimes even addictive?
At first, I thought the loop was just a clever gimmick. Then I realized the loop changes what “progress” means. In

, I don’t really get stronger. I don’t grind for better gear. Most of the time, I die and come back with nothing. And yet I’m still moving forward—because the thing that grows is not my character, it’s my understanding.
That shift is powerful. In many games, failure feels like losing. In

, failure often feels like data. I didn’t “waste” a run—I ran an experiment. I learned what happens when I arrive earlier, or when I wait, or when I take a different path. The reset stops being a punishment and becomes a rhythm: try, observe, revise.

The time limit also does something subtle to my attention. When I know I only have a short window, I stop wandering aimlessly. I start caring about minutes. I start making plans. It’s not just “where should I go,” but “what can I realistically learn before the world resets?” That pressure could have been stressful, but for me it often becomes focus. I’m not drowning in infinite options. I’m choosing one question to chase right now.

And the best part is the feeling of a real breakthrough. The kind of moment where you’re not following a waypoint—you’re connecting dots in your head. You read something, you see something, you remember something from three loops ago, and suddenly the world makes sense in a new way. It’s a very specific pleasure: the pleasure of
That’s why the loop doesn’t feel like repetition to me.
The planet may repeat, but I don’t.
Each loop is like rewatching the same scene with new context: the same events, but a different interpretation. The world becomes a clockwork system, and I’m slowly learning how it ticks.
What makes this even more memorable is how well the mechanic matches the theme.

is a story about curiosity across an impossible scale of time—different civilizations, ruins, endings you cannot prevent, questions that outlive you. The loop makes those ideas emotional instead of abstract. I don’t just read that time is unstoppable—I feel it every run. And strangely, that doesn’t make the experience hopeless. It makes it meaningful. Because if the ending is guaranteed, then the value shifts to the act of seeking truth anyway.
So if I had to summarize why fixed-time loops work (at least for me), it’s this:
A good time loop turns repetition into intention.
And it turns exploration into understanding.
I’m curious how other players feel. Do you like time loops because they’re efficient and structured, or because they create that “aha” feeling? And what was your most unforgettable
moment—the moment you realized you weren’t just exploring space, you were learning a system?
